title: Celebrity Culture Predicted Fertility Decline in Japan and South Korea
gist: Peter Foreshaw Brookes and Lyman Stone argue that the timing of Japan's (mid-1980s) and South Korea's (early 1990s) fertility declines is better explained by the rise of 'idol' celebrity culture — celebrities who hide romantic/family life and foster parasocial bonds — than by economic shocks like the 1973 Oil Crisis, Plaza Accord, or Asian Financial Crisis. Their Baby Nudges survey links admiring a large-family celebrity to a 14% higher chance of intending another child, and they suggest governments could nudge celebrity culture toward familism.

insights.claim: Japan's fertility decline beginning around 1973 was not unusual: Western countries began declining in the 1960s alongside their sexual revolutions, and Japan's sexual revolution started in the early 1970s.
insights.speaker: Peter Foreshaw Brookes and Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Fertility turns track norm changes around coupling and family, not just economic cycles.

themes.theme: Idol culture as a fertility driver

insights.claim: Japan's celebrity 'idol culture' exploded after an expansion of TV channels, color TV and audition-based gameshows in the late 1970s, and especially after satellite TV rolled out in mid-1984, coinciding with the fertility departure.
insights.speaker: Peter Foreshaw Brookes and Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Media-technology shifts can have demographic second-order effects — relevant to today's social-media/streaming debates.

insights.claim: Japanese idols were expected to appear emotionally available while minimizing discussion of their own romantic and family lives, a norm that has since spread across Asian celebrity culture.

insights.claim: South Korea's Japan-style idol culture arguably began in 1992 with Seo Taiji's band; Taiji kept his 1993 relationship and later marriage secret until divorce proceedings.

insights.claim: The authors predict governments could design nudges to generate familistic celebrities, making visible family life among cultural leaders a pronatal policy tool.

insights.so_what: Watch for pronatalist governments (e.g., Korea) experimenting with media/celebrity-based family promotion.
